newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST- BLS seasonals may mask solid US May jobs.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST- BLS seasonals may mask solid US May jobs.

text.p: New seasonal adjustment factors from the Bureau of Labor Statistics should dampen the rise in U.S. payrolls for May, but many economists are still banking on a robust job market heading into the summer months.
Forecasters scrambled to adjust down their estimates for the headline jobs figure -- some by as much as 100,000 --following release of the revised seasonals last Friday.

According to a Reuters poll conducted on Tuesday, they are now expecting a gain of 219,000 in May non-farm jobs, up from 142,000 in April, when the closely watched report is released this Friday, June 6 at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT.

"Several factors argue for a bounceback even given these new seasonals and one of them is the weather which was exceptionally poor in April," said Richard Berner, chief economist at Pittsburgh-based Mellon Bank.
"Generally speaking, all the indicators that we look at to gauge what's going on in the labor market suggest that we strengthened in May."
Berner, who said that a five-week survey period during the month of May could add 30,000 or more to the non-farm jobs number, expects a gain of 285,000.
Whether a strong report will be enough to sway a watchful Federal Reserve into pushing up official interest rates again at their next meeting in early July is still an open question.

The unemployment rate, which fell to a 23-year low of 4.9 percent last month, and the average hourly earnings figure, which is expected to rise a healthy 0.4 percent in May, will be closely scrutinized by policymakers, economists said.

Overall manufacturing hours, which matched a post-World War II high of 42.2 hours in April, and overtime, which moved up to 5.0 hours, its highest level since the series began in 1956, will also garner interest.
But with scant signs of consumer inflation present, many believe that strong labor market growth alone will not be enough to prompt tighter credit.

"The unemployment rate is important but at the end of the day even the employment data is not as important as the strength of consumer spending and inflation news," said Bill Dudley, chief U.S. economist at Goldman Sachs.
Dudley expects the jobless level to tick back up to 5.0 percent in May -- in line with consensus forecasts -- but said he could not rule out a steady rate or another surprise decline.
"There's a lot of uncertainty about what the unemployment rate is going to do because it's hard to know if last month's decline was catch-up or not," he said.
The non-farm payroll data are based on a survey of employers, and the jobless rate and other civilian employment data are based on a survey of households.

Regardless of the implications of Friday's report for near-term Fed policy, market watchers predicted that the numbers will almost certainly give a clear reading on an expected second quarter slowdown.
Jobs performance is often a harbinger of consumer behavior, economists said, and could provide clues about the direction of other May indicators.

"Payrolls are very often the first indication of the direction that the rest of data in the month will take, especially when you have weather effects," said Christopher Low, senior economist at HSBC Markets.
"If you see strong demand in the employment report chances are you'll see it elsewhere."
